title: But what is the Fourier Transform?  A visual introduction.
summary: 3Blue1Brown's animated visual introduction to the Fourier Transform, showing how a signal breaks into frequency components.
why_hn: HN's default recommendation for understanding the Fourier transform intuitively; many say it was the explanation that made it click.

title: What Happened to Horses Is Happening to Us
summary: CGP Grey's video "Humans Need Not Apply" argues that automation will make a large part of the workforce economically obsolete, much as engines did for horses. It surveys robots and software replacing both physical and mental labor.
why_hn: HN has recommended it for a decade as the standard explainer on automation and unemployment, though skeptics later cite it as an example of overconfident predictions.

title: USENIX Security '18-Q: Why Do Keynote Speakers Keep Suggesting That Improving Security Is Possible?
summary: James Mickens's humorous USENIX Security keynote argues that improving security and trusting opaque technology like machine learning is far harder than the industry admits.
why_hn: HN considers it a classic, hilarious and sobering talk on ML inscrutability and tech hubris, often rewatched.

title: Computer program that learns to play classic NES games
summary: Tom7 explains and demos software that learns to play NES games by finding score patterns in memory and then searching for inputs that raise it. It is the video companion to his SIGBOVIK paper.
why_hn: Loved on HN as a hilarious, brilliant example of hacker-academic work and cited whenever game-playing AI or fuzzing comes up.

title: Is Most Published Research Wrong?
summary: Veritasium explains why a large share of published research findings may be false, covering p-values, p-hacking, publication bias and low replication rates. It draws on John Ioannidis's well-known paper and describes reforms such as preregistration.
why_hn: HN commenters link it whenever a shaky study or the p<0.05 threshold comes up, as a short primer on false positives in science.

title: Essence of linear algebra preview
summary: A five-minute preview of 3Blue1Brown's Essence of Linear Algebra series, which uses animation to build geometric intuition for topics from a standard linear algebra course.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends the series as the best intuition-first, visual introduction to linear algebra and a benchmark for clear math explanation.

title: "Voice Driven Development: Who needs a keyboard anyway?" by Emily Shea
summary: Emily Shea explains how repetitive strain injury pushed her to program by voice using speech recognition (Talon), and gives a live coding demo. She argues voice-driven development can be pain-free, efficient and enjoyable.
why_hn: It is the go-to recommendation whenever someone asks about voice coding or RSI-friendly programming setups.

title: Veritasium: What Everyone Gets Wrong About AI and Learning – Derek Muller Explains
summary: Veritasium's Derek Muller gives a Perimeter Institute livestream on how AI might change teaching and learning. He draws on past technology shifts and cognitive science to argue that learning requires effortful repetition.
why_hn: Recommended as a balanced take on AI and education, with the point that learning takes work that no technology can do for you.

title: (1/4) Intro/History: Introducing a 100-year-old mechanical computer
summary: The first of four short videos from Bill Hammack (engineerguy) introducing and giving the history of a 100-year-old mechanical computer, Michelson's harmonic analyzer. The series goes on to explain Fourier synthesis, analysis and operation of the machine.
why_hn: Commenters recommend the series whenever Fourier analysis or analog computing comes up, praising Hammack's clear explanations and the short episodes.

title: Tensorflow and deep learning - without a PhD by Martin Görner
summary: Martin Gorner's Devoxx talk introduces deep learning with TensorFlow, walking through neural networks for MNIST, how to choose an architecture and how to diagnose networks that fail to train.
why_hn: Repeatedly called an excellent, practical introduction that covers a lot in two hours and explains issues academic textbooks skip.

title: The more general uncertainty principle, regarding Fourier transforms
summary: 3Blue1Brown shows how the uncertainty principle arises from Fourier transforms. A wave packet cannot be narrow in both position and frequency, so the principle is a property of waves rather than of measurement.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the clearest visual explanation that uncertainty is intrinsic to waves, separate from measurement disturbance.

title: Robocalypse Now: Using Deep Learning to Combat Cheating in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive
summary: Valve's John McDonald presents at GDC 2018 on how Valve uses deep learning (VACnet) to detect cheaters in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. He covers training on human-reviewed replays and how model output is confirmed by manual review.
why_hn: The go-to link in any anti-cheat thread for a concrete, well-delivered account of machine-learning cheat detection in production.

title: Michael Stonebraker | Big Data is (at least) Four Different Problems
summary: Database pioneer Michael Stonebraker argues that 'big data' is really at least four different problems: big volumes with small analytics, big analytics, velocity, and variety. He comments on where each market is heading.
why_hn: HN points to it as a thoughtful, first-principles take from a Turing award winner that cuts through NoSQL and big data hype.

title: Special Topics - The Kalman Filter (1 of 55) What is a Kalman Filter?
summary: The first video in a 55-part series by Michel van Biezen that introduces the Kalman filter and builds from the rationale through algebraic examples to the full matrix treatment. The videos are short, blackboard-style lectures.
why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends this series as a clear, step-by-step way to really understand Kalman filtering.

title: Intro to AI Safety, Remastered
summary: Robert Miles gives a remastered introduction to AI safety, adapted from a talk in London. It lays out why advanced AI could go wrong and answers common objections.
why_hn: The default link for newcomers wanting an approachable, entertaining introduction to AI risk and alignment.

title: Why Not Just: Think of AGI Like a Corporation?
summary: Robert Miles asks whether corporations can be thought of as artificial general superintelligences and how far the analogy holds. He argues the differences, such as being limited by employees' capabilities, matter for AI safety.
why_hn: HN points to it as an accessible rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just corporate risk.

title: Attention in transformers, step-by-step | Deep Learning Chapter 6
summary: 3Blue1Brown's visual walkthrough of the attention mechanism inside transformers, covering self-attention, multiple heads and cross-attention. It is chapter 6 of his deep learning series.
why_hn: HN treats it as the go-to visual explanation of attention, recommended to people who find text-based transformer explainers hard to follow.

title: Slaughterbots
summary: Slaughterbots is a fictional short film, backed by Stuart Russell, depicting swarms of cheap autonomous drones that use facial recognition to assassinate targets. It was made to argue for banning autonomous weapons.
why_hn: HN invokes it as the standard reference whenever drone swarms, autonomous weapons or military AI come up in the news.

title: Democrats Need to Face Why Trump Won | The Ezra Klein Show
summary: Ezra Klein interviews Democratic pollster David Shor, who walks through survey data and charts explaining the 2024 election results. They discuss voter shifts, the education divide and what Democrats got wrong.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a data-driven explanation of the 2024 election and voter trends.

title: The medical test paradox, and redesigning Bayes' rule
summary: 3Blue1Brown explains why positive results on accurate medical tests are often false positives, and reframes Bayes' rule using likelihood ratios (Bayes factors) to update odds. It uses visual examples to make the reasoning intuitive.
why_hn: HN's go-to link whenever Bayesian reasoning, base rates or imperfect tests come up.

title: Keynote: Begin...End?
summary: David Beazley's PyData Global 2021 keynote, an oral history of early scientific Python. He tells how Python ended up running on a Connection Machine supercomputer at Los Alamos.
why_hn: Cited in threads about Python's rise as a first-hand, entertaining account of why it won in scientific computing.

title: Is AI Safety a Pascal's Mugging?
summary: Robert Miles examines whether the case for AI safety is a Pascal's mugging, a tiny probability of an enormous payoff. He argues it is not, because AI risk does not depend on vanishingly small probabilities.
why_hn: HN points to it as a reasoned rebuttal to the claim that AI risk is just Pascal's wager.

title: Hans Rosling: Debunking third-world myths with the best stats you've ever seen
summary: In this TED talk, Hans Rosling uses animated statistics to debunk myths about the developing world, showing how health and income have improved across countries.
why_hn: Cited as the classic data-driven argument that the first-world versus third-world split is outdated and the world is improving.

title: Lower Latency Graph Queries in Cypher with Redis GraphRoi Lipman, Redis LabsTim Davis, Texas A&M U
summary: Redis Labs and Tim Davis present RedisGraph, which uses GraphBLAS to treat graph queries in Cypher as sparse linear algebra for lower latency.
why_hn: Recommended in graph database threads as a mind-blowing case for expressing graph analysis as linear algebra.

title: Connections between physics and deep learning
summary: Max Tegmark's MIT CBMM talk on why deep learning works so well. He argues that the laws of physics and the symmetries in physical data make it compressible into small neural networks, tying physics to network structure.
why_hn: HN recommends it as a clear argument for why deep and cheap learning succeeds, often alongside the associated paper.

title: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn | Deep Learning Chapter 2
summary: 3Blue1Brown's second neural network chapter explains cost functions and gradient descent, showing how a network learns by minimizing error during training.
why_hn: HN recommends the series as a very accessible way to understand the math behind machine learning and LLMs.

title: Lecture 1: Probability and Counting | Statistics 110
summary: Lecture 1 of Harvard's Statistics 110 with Joe Blitzstein, introducing sample spaces, the naive definition of probability, counting, binomial coefficients and the sampling table.
why_hn: Recommended on Ask HN threads as a high-quality free probability course for relearning math or building an ML foundation.

title: GDC 2010: Sid Meier Keynote - "Everything You Know is Wrong"
summary: Sid Meier's GDC 2010 keynote on how players perceive probability in games, including how Civilization's odds were adjusted because players misjudged them.
why_hn: HN points to it as the best talk on how people misunderstand probabilities and how designers handle that.

title: Do we need Attention? - Linear RNNs and State Space Models (SSMs) for NLP
summary: Sasha Rush surveys linear RNNs and state space models as replacements for attention in transformer-style models, in a talk for MLSys. It covers the foundational preliminaries and predates Mamba.
why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for building intuition about state space models and the tradeoffs between transformer and SSM layers.

title: What 40,000 Videos Tell Us About The Trending Tab
summary: Coffee Break analyzes about 40,000 videos from seven months of YouTube's trending tab. It examines whether trending is biased toward mainstream media and late-night shows.
why_hn: Cited in threads on YouTube algorithms and creator complaints as a data-driven look at the trending tab.

title: Google Developers Day US - Theorizing from Data
summary: Peter Norvig's 2007 Google talk on theorizing from data, covering what huge datasets can do for language understanding, translation, information extraction and inference. It argues that more data often beats cleverer models.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the clear explanation of why Google's statistical, data-first approach works.

title: The Best (and Worst) Ways to Shuffle Cards - Numberphile
summary: Persi Diaconis explains on Numberphile the mathematics of card shuffling, including why seven riffle shuffles are needed to randomize a deck and how different shuffles compare.
why_hn: HN points to it as a good, anecdote-filled introduction to the math of shuffling from the expert himself.

title: RAAIS 2017 - Simon Knowles, Co-Founder and CTO of Graphcore
channel: The Research and Applied AI Summit - RAAIS
summary: Simon Knowles, co-founder and CTO of Graphcore, talks about "intelligence processors", chips designed specifically for machine learning. The talk was given at the RAAIS 2017 summit and covers Graphcore's architecture.
why_hn: HN points to it as a technical talk from a chip designer on why AI hardware should put memory close to compute and use async data transfers.

title: Jake Vanderplas - Statistics for Hackers - PyCon 2016.mp4
summary: Jake Vanderplas's PyCon 2016 talk shows how sampling-based methods such as simulation, shuffling and bootstrapping make statistics intuitive. His pitch is that if you can write a for-loop, you can do statistics.
why_hn: It is recommended to programmers who want to learn statistics through simulation rather than memorized formulas.

title: Tesla Autonomy Day
summary: Tesla's roughly four-hour Autonomy Day investor event covers its in-house self-driving chip, vision-only approach, fleet data engine and robotaxi plans, with talks by Andrej Karpathy and others.
why_hn: Cited both as a primary source on Tesla's technical autonomy approach and, later, for Musk's unmet robotaxi predictions.

title: Dance p 3 Mar09
summary: Geoff Cumming uses a simulation to show how wildly the p value varies from one replication to the next because of sampling variability. He argues for estimation and confidence intervals over null hypothesis significance testing.
why_hn: Recommended as a vivid visual demonstration of how unreliable p-values are.

title: Speaking Piano - Now with (somewhat decent) captions!
summary: A player piano is made to reproduce human speech, here reciting a European Environmental Criminal Court proclamation in German at the 2009 World Venice Forum. This upload adds subtitles so the words become understandable.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the canonical talking-piano example, uncanny and impressive once you read the captions.

title: This AI actually WORKS!!! - NVIDIA RTX Voice
summary: A ShortCircuit (Linus Tech Tips) review of Nvidia's RTX Voice, which uses GPU-based neural networks to remove background noise from microphone audio. It demonstrates how well the filtering works.
why_hn: Cited as a demo of GPU-powered noise suppression that works remarkably well, in threads on mic muting and speech enhancement.

title: BahnMining - Pünktlichkeit ist eine Zier (David Kriesel)
summary: David Kriesel's 36C3 talk, in German, analyzes a year of scraped data on every stop of every long-distance train in Germany. It shows how Deutsche Bahn delay statistics hide cancellations and delays.
why_hn: Recommended in threads on German rail as the data-backed explanation of how reported punctuality understates real delays.

title: Practical Deep Learning for Coders: Lesson 1
summary: Lesson 1 of fast.ai's Practical Deep Learning for Coders, taught by Jeremy Howard. It takes coders from running code in a Jupyter notebook straight into training a real image model.
why_hn: HN considers the course one of the best hands-on ways into deep learning, praising the code-first teaching style.

title: Bayes theorem, the geometry of changing beliefs
summary: 3Blue1Brown presents Bayes' theorem through a geometric diagram, showing how evidence should update beliefs. It works through the Kahneman and Tversky style questions and base rates.
why_hn: HN people recommend it as the most intuitive introduction to Bayes' theorem and cite it in base-rate arguments.

title: Lecture 1 | Convex Optimization I (Stanford)
summary: The introductory lecture of Stephen Boyd's Stanford Convex Optimization I course (EE 364A). It outlines convex sets, functions and problems, and the course's coverage of least-squares, linear and semidefinite programming, duality and interior-point methods.
why_hn: HN recommends Boyd's lectures as a fantastic, often funny follow-up to linear algebra and as a step in machine learning study paths.

title: Militarizing Your Backyard with Python: Computer Vision and the Squirrel Hordes
summary: A PyCon 2012 talk by Kurt Grandis on building an automated water-squirting turret that uses Python and computer vision to detect and drive off squirrels from a bird feeder.
why_hn: HN loves it as a funny, inspiring hobby project and calls it one of the best conference talks ever.

title: Cambridge Ideas - Professor Risk
summary: David Spiegelhalter, Professor of the Public Understanding of Risk, uses statistics to weigh everyday risks such as bacon sandwiches and cycling. The six-minute piece introduces micromorts as a way to compare the risk of dying.
why_hn: Recommended as a short, fun introduction to micromorts and thinking about risk.

title: HC2023-K2: Hardware for Deep Learning
summary: Bill Dally of NVIDIA gives a Hot Chips 2023 keynote on the challenges of building hardware for deep learning. He traces how GPUs have been adapted for machine learning, especially training.
why_hn: HN points to it for an insider view of why NVIDIA's AI gains came from design rather than process, and for data-movement power costs.

title: Why ChatGPT Can't Draw a Full Glass of Wine
summary: Alex O'Connor shows that ChatGPT cannot draw a wine glass filled to the brim, and ties the failure to David Hume's missing shade of blue. It asks what the failure says about how image models learn.
why_hn: HN treats it as the origin of the full-wine-glass meme and an illustration of how models lack concepts missing from their training data.

title: AI can't cross this line and we don't know why.
summary: A Welch Labs explainer on neural scaling laws and the compute-efficient frontier, asking why model loss seems to hit a line it cannot cross. It draws an analogy to an ideal gas law for AI.
why_hn: Recommended as a well-made, digestible introduction to scaling laws and why models cluster along a similar efficiency frontier.

title: 10 Reasons to Ignore AI Safety
summary: Robert Miles goes through ten common reasons people give for dismissing AI safety, adapted from Stuart Russell's list, and answers each one. It is aimed at skeptics and newcomers.
why_hn: HN commenters link it as a compact rebuttal to dismissive arguments and as a way to see why people consider AI safety important.

title: #VoCo. Adobe Audio Manipulator Sneak Peak with Jordan Peele | Adobe Creative Cloud
summary: Adobe's VoCo demo from the MAX 2016 Sneak Peeks, co-hosted by Jordan Peele, showing software that changes words in a voiceover by typing new ones.
why_hn: HN cites it as the early example of voice cloning and audio deepfakes, with some recommending Peele's reaction and others calling the demo fake or never shipped.

title: OpenAI Plays Hide and Seek…and Breaks The Game! 🤖
summary: Two Minute Papers covers OpenAI's multi-agent hide-and-seek experiment, in which agents learned emergent tool use and found ways to break the game's rules. It summarizes the 'Emergent Tool Use from Multi-Agent Interaction' paper.
why_hn: HN mentions it as a fun and slightly worrying example of AI systems behaving in unintended ways when optimizing.

title: The Bayesian Trap
summary: Veritasium explains Bayes' theorem with examples and introduces the 'Bayesian trap', where repeated events get mistaken for inevitable ones. It discusses how priors shape our expectations and behavior.
why_hn: HN points to it as an accessible introduction to Bayesian reasoning and as inspiration for personal projects.

title: The Man behind Stable Diffusion
summary: Yannic Kilcher interviews Emad Mostaque, founder of Stability AI, about the company's funding, its mission, and the release of Stable Diffusion. Topics include access to compute, handling harmful outputs, and avoiding the corrupting influence of profit.
why_hn: Commenters cite it during Stable Diffusion release debates as a source for Mostaque's vision and Stability's principles.

title: Daniel Schmachtenberger on The Portal (with host Eric Weinstein), Ep. #027 - On Avoiding Apocalypses
summary: A long conversation between Eric Weinstein and Daniel Schmachtenberger on whether humanity can flourish long term on a single planet, introducing the Game A versus Game B framing. It covers catastrophic risk and alternatives to rivalrous systems.
why_hn: Commenters recommend the whole interview as a wide-ranging discussion of existential risk.

title: BetrFS: A Right-Optimized Write-Optimized File System
summary: A Microsoft Research talk on BetrFS, a file system built on B-epsilon trees, a write-optimized data structure. It covers WODS such as LSM-trees, how to design a file system around them, and benchmark wins over ext4 and xfs.
why_hn: HN points to it as a solid, if long, introduction to B-epsilon trees and why BetrFS is built the way it is.

title: How AI Could Save (Not Destroy) Education | Sal Khan | TED
summary: Sal Khan of Khan Academy gives a TED talk on how AI could transform education, with a personal tutor for every student and a teaching assistant for every teacher. He demos Khanmigo, including features where the AI reasons before responding.
why_hn: Cited in AI-and-education threads as the optimistic case and demo for AI tutoring, and as a source on Khan Academy's LLM approach.

title: Cursor Team: Future of Programming with AI | Lex Fridman Podcast #447
summary: A Lex Fridman podcast conversation with the four creators of Cursor, the AI-assisted code editor. They discuss how the editor integrates models into programming workflows, including custom completion models and techniques like speculative decoding to speed up applying edits.
why_hn: HN commenters point to it as the best first-hand account of Cursor's technical internals, straight from its founders.

title: Why Can't AI Make Its Own Discoveries? — With Yann LeCun
summary: Yann LeCun on the Big Technology Podcast discusses why current AI models cannot make discoveries despite their knowledge. He argues systems need abstract world models and also covers limits of AI research, investor expectations, and open source after DeepSeek.
why_hn: Pointed to as LeCun's argument for the limits of LLMs and the need for world models.

title: Backpropagation calculus | Deep Learning Chapter 4
summary: 3Blue1Brown's chapter 4 on deep learning gives a more formal, symbol-based account of backpropagation calculus, connecting the intuition from the previous chapter to the math found in textbooks and code.
why_hn: Recommended as an accessible, visual way to understand backpropagation and neural networks.

title: Lecture 1 | Introduction to Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition
summary: The first lecture of Stanford's CS231n course on convolutional neural networks for visual recognition. It surveys the history and key challenges of computer vision, from the Cambrian explosion and Hubel and Wiesel to ImageNet.
why_hn: HN recommends the CS231n lectures as a solid, applied deep learning course for self-study.

title: The Lighthill Debate (1973) - part 1 of 6
summary: First part of a six-part recording of the 1973 Lighthill debate on AI, where Sir James Lighthill's critical report on AI research was contested by figures including McCarthy and Michie.
why_hn: Recommended as a historical look at the AI winter debate and a demolition of the expert systems hype.

title: Autonomous Car - what goes into sensing for autonomous driving?
summary: Mobileye co-founder and CTO Amnon Shashua explains what goes into sensing for autonomous driving and whether end-to-end deep learning can work for it. He argues for decomposing the problem.
why_hn: Recommended as an accessible technical explanation of Mobileye's approach, and also cited in disputes over Tesla Autopilot.

title: What is Euler's formula actually saying? | Ep. 4 Lockdown live math
summary: A 3Blue1Brown live lockdown math episode asking what Euler's formula e^(pi i) is actually saying. It builds intuition through exponentials, rotation and vectors landing on the unit circle.
why_hn: HN recommends it as the explanation that makes complex exponentials click, especially for understanding the Fourier transform.

title: Facebook's Prototype VR Face Tracking Got Even Better
summary: UploadVR covers a Facebook Reality Labs prototype that tracks facial expressions using cameras mounted in a VR headset. The updated version captures subtle micro-expressions for realistic avatars.
why_hn: Pointed to in metaverse and VR threads as proof that realtime photorealistic face tracking from headset cameras is coming.

title: High-Speed Robot Hand
summary: A short demo from the Ishikawa Komuro Lab of a high-speed robot hand paired with a 1000fps vision system performing dexterous manipulation. It shows what very low-latency vision and actuation can do.
why_hn: HN cites it as an example of what 1kHz vision and fast control loops enable, in threads about AI hardware and robotics.

title: Building Brains to Understand the World's Data
summary: Jeff Hawkins presents his view that the neocortex works on principles different from traditional computers. He describes sparse distributed representations and how they are learned, then shows how Numenta applies them to predict from high-velocity data streams.
why_hn: Recommended as Hawkins' own accessible statement of his brain-inspired theory of intelligence and its software implementation.

title: Jim Keller - Moore's Law in the age of AI Chips
summary: Jim Keller's talk at the 2020 Scaled Machine Learning conference on Moore's Law in the age of AI chips. He compares scalar, vector and GPU-style parallel approaches to computation.
why_hn: Cited in hardware threads as a Keller talk on the different ways of doing parallel processing.

title: GradIEEEnt half decent: The hidden power of imprecise lines
summary: Tom 7 (suckerpinch) delivers a long, comedic digression on gradient descent and floating-point imprecision. He shows how rounding behavior can supply the nonlinearity needed to build a neural network.
why_hn: Cited as a fun, unconventional example of neural networks built from floating point error.

title: The Visual Microphone: Passive Recovery of Sound from Video
summary: MIT researchers show that sound can be recovered from silent video by analyzing tiny vibrations in objects such as a potato chip bag. It works even with consumer cameras by using rolling shutter.
why_hn: HN commenters cite it as the classic demonstration of audio recovery from video in surveillance and privacy discussions.

title: Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again)
summary: Andrej Karpathy's keynote at AI Startup School laying out software 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0, with LLMs seen as utilities, fabs and operating systems. It covers LLM quirks, partial-autonomy apps and keeping a human in the generate-and-verify loop.
why_hn: HN mostly cites it as a source for Karpathy's framing of programming in English and his generate-then-verify workflow, with a few critics finding it hype.

title: Speech Recognition Breakthrough for the Spoken, Translated Word
summary: Microsoft Research's Rick Rashid demonstrates a speech recognition and translation system, built on deep neural networks, that turns his spoken English into Chinese speech in 2012.
why_hn: HN cites it as an early impressive real-time speech translation demo, often in discussions of voice-preserving translation and later AI demos.

title: VACNET Anti-cheat
summary: 3kliksphilip summarizes Valve's GDC talk on VACNet, a deep-learning system that flags CS:GO cheaters and feeds the Overwatch review queue. It covers Trust Factor, VAC, and how the data is collected and analyzed.
why_hn: HN cites it as a source for how Valve uses machine learning on player behavior to detect cheating.

title: Imaging at a trillion frames per second | Ramesh Raskar
summary: Ramesh Raskar presents femto-photography, a technique that captures a trillion frames per second, fast enough to show light itself moving through a scene. He discusses possible uses such as cameras that see around corners or inside the body.
why_hn: HN points to it as the clearest and most striking explanation of femto-photography, with animations that make it easy to follow whenever related imaging stories appear.

title: Intelligence is not Enough | Bryan Cantrill | Monktoberfest 2023
summary: Bryan Cantrill's Monktoberfest 2023 talk takes on AI doomerism, weighing the theoretical existential risks against the reality on the ground. He takes a skeptical but thoughtful view of how to balance AI's potential against its risks.
why_hn: Recommended as a thoughtful Cantrill talk on embracing failure and curiosity in engineering, and as a skeptical counterpoint to AI doom narratives.

title: [60 fps]  A Trip Through Paris, France in late 1890s / Un voyage à travers Paris, 1890
summary: Denis Shiryaev's neural-network-upscaled, colorized 60 fps version of film footage shot in Paris between 1896 and 1900.
why_hn: HN cites it for the look of pre-car city streets, with pedestrians moving freely among carriages, and as an example of AI film restoration.

title: Richard Feynman: Can Machines Think?
summary: An excerpt of Richard Feynman's 1985 lecture Q&A about whether machines can think. He discusses the difficulty of defining what computers can never do and compares machine intelligence to machines that don't copy animals.
why_hn: HN uses it as an early authoritative take in debates about AI, reasoning, and AGI.

title: Movie reconstruction from human brain activity
summary: Jack Gallant's lab demonstrates reconstructing movie trailer clips a subject watched from fMRI brain activity, using regression models trained on hours of viewing data. The video shows the original clip beside the reconstruction.
why_hn: HN cites it as the landmark brain-decoding demo and compares newer reconstruction work against it.

title: Reveal Invisible Motion With This Clever Video Trick
summary: Steve Mould explains motion amplification and video magnification, techniques that find tiny changes in video invisible to the eye and exaggerate them. He covers the MIT research and industrial uses such as diagnosing vibrating machinery.
why_hn: Pointed to as an approachable layperson's explanation whenever video magnification or vibration visualization comes up.

title: Ken Stanley: Discovery Without Objectives
summary: A 92-minute RMIT University seminar in which Ken Stanley argues that setting an objective can block achieving it. He presents objective-less, novelty-driven search as an alternative approach to innovation and discovery, drawing on evolutionary computation.
why_hn: Cited as a source for the idea that open-ended search can beat objective-driven optimization, though one commenter found parts of it fluffy.

title: Experiences Building Edge TPU with Chisel
summary: A Google talk from the Chisel community in which engineers recount designing the Edge TPU with the Chisel hardware construction language. It covers the productivity gains and the problems they hit.
why_hn: Pointed to as a rare first-hand account of a real, shipping ASIC built in an open-source HDL, useful in HDL and FPGA choice discussions.
